original_wisa_caption:
The video begins with a close-up shot of a vibrant orange, textured object that resembles a piece of coral or a sponge. The object is irregularly shaped and has a rough, fibrous surface with small specks of blue and green scattered throughout. As the camera slowly zooms in, the texture becomes more pronounced, revealing intricate details of the fibers and the subtle variations in color. The background remains dark, which accentuates the bright orange hue of the object.

As the camera continues to move closer, the object transforms into what appears to be a piece of coral or a similar marine organism. The texture and color remain consistent, but the shape starts to take on a more defined form. The camera then shifts focus to a different part of the scene, where a red, gelatinous substance is shown. This substance has a smooth, glossy surface and a translucent quality, with a small black hole visible near its center. The camera zooms in further, highlighting the fluid-like nature of the substance
caption: A macro close-up frames a fuzzy, fibrous reddish-pink mound rising against a near-black background. The framing remains essentially fixed, and tiny bright specks dot the upper ridge as the gloss spreads. A small blue circular spot rests near the center of the mound, while bluish-green fringes line its lower edges. The surface is already wetting and shifting at the start, and this slow change continues without resolution. On the right side, a darker-red bulge gradually smooths into a glossier, more dome-like form. At the lower center, a pale amber feature gains a clearer droplet highlight over time, taking on a fuller sheen. The overall exposure drifts too: the mound reads more orange-pink at first and deepens into a more saturated red with stronger specular glints later. These local surface changes unfold steadily, while the central blue spot and the blue-green base fringes stay in place, marking one continuous, unresolved moment of a slow wetting process.

endpoints are normal, not physical errors. Do not add unseen causes, onset, stopping or outcomes.
An internal editing cut is not evidence of physical motion connecting the views.

Check identification before physical interpretation: a reflection is not a separate actor;
a powder/smoke/liquid outline or shadow is not automatically the boundary of a solid object;
an apparent change caused by occlusion/viewpoint is not automatically material deformation.

the appropriate material/surface itself provides visible evidence. Do not infer a force or earlier
collision just because the visible configuration would be compatible with it.

claims of stillness, no motion, no camera motion or 'exactly' synchronized changes.

processes. Avoid deleting the real process merely because its cause lies outside the cropped window.
